https://sana.sy/en/politics/2341616/.text: Saudi Arabia, Jordan, UK and Denmark welcome IAEA decision on Syria Capitals, Sept. 9 (SANA) Saudi Arabia , Jordan , the United Kingdom and Denmark on Wednesday welcomed a decision by the International Atomic Energy Agency ( IAEA ) Board of Governors to remove the Syria -related “noncompliance” item from its agenda, citing positive developments in the file and Syria’s cooperation with the agency. In a statement, the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs welcomed the consensus reached by the IAEA Board of Governors on the decision submitted by Saudi Arabia, as chair of the Arab Group in Vienna, together with Jordan, Egypt and Morocco. The ministry said the decision reflects support for the positive developments concerning Syria’s nuclear file. Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its support for Syria and for efforts and steps aimed at strengthening its security, stability and sovereignty and supporting its national institutions, contributing to the Syrian people’s aspirations for a future of security, stability and prosperity. Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates also welcomed the Board of Governors’ adoption of the decision concerning Syria, which ended the board’s consideration of the implementation of the safeguards agreement in Syria in light of the country’s full cooperation with the IAEA. The United Kingdom’s Special Envoy for Syria, Barrie Peach, welcomed the decision, saying it reflects Syria’s cooperation on outstanding nuclear-related issues dating back to the Assad era. He said the UK welcomed the step, which would contribute to strengthening transparency, international engagement and nuclear nonproliferation. After 15 years, the UK welcomes @iaeaorg ’s consensus decision to remove Syria from its list of non-compliant states, reflecting 🇸🇾's cooperation on outstanding Assad-era nuclear issues. A positive step for transparency, engagement, and non-proliferation. — Barrie Peach, UK Special Representative for Syria (@UKSyriaRep) September 9, 2026 Denmark likewise welcomed the IAEA Board’s decision to remove the Syria-related noncompliance item from its agenda, describing it as an important step toward strengthening the global nuclear nonproliferation regime. Danish Ambassador to International Organizations in Vienna Christian Grønbech-Jensen said the decision represented an important milestone and recognized Syria’s cooperation with the IAEA and its director general. https://business-review.eu/business-revi.text: FIS 2026 highlights: Industrial growth in Romania increasingly depends on technology, talent and regional competitiveness Romania remains well placed to attract industrial investment, but its ability to compete will increasingly depend on technology, infrastructure, workforce quality and the capacity to adapt existing assets to new economic realities, business leaders said at Foreign Investors Summit 2026. The discussion brought together Geanina Ungureanu, Head of Retail at CPI Romania; Tiberiu Danetiu, Director for Corporate Affairs & Retail Media at Auchan Romania; Lucian Enaru, Country General Manager at Schneider Electric; İlker Kuşoğlu, Senior Vice President at Bosch; and Gijs Klomp, Business Development Manager at WDP. The session was moderated by Ștefan Surcel, Head of Industrial Agency at Cushman & Wakefield Echinox Romania. Retail investment moves towards adaptation rather than simple expansion For CPI Romania, one of the defining themes is the transformation of existing retail properties. Geanina Ungureanu noted that the group has assets throughout Romania and has increasingly focused on refurbishing shopping centres that have already been operating for close to two decades. Read more about Auchan announces first immersive LED display in Romanian retail sector, at Auchan Drumul Taberei read more “Retail spaces have to be constantly adapted to remain relevant. At Sun Plaza, we are opening a new 18,000 sqm GLA wing on 26 November, bringing in Auchan, Primark, Reserved and other partners.” The redevelopment illustrates a wider shift in retail formats. Large spaces previously occupied by a single hypermarket are increasingly being reconfigured to accommodate a broader mix of tenants and consumer uses. “A format that worked years ago may no longer work today, so refurbishment and repositioning are essential.” Ungureanu also pointed to the evolution of Central European capital in Romania, with CPI’s portfolio moving from Austrian to Czech ownership and demonstrating that increasingly large investments are also coming from within the region. Auchan highlights the local economy behind international investment Tiberiu Danetiu described Auchan’s more than two decades in Romania as a story that increasingly combines international capital with local sourcing, management and workforce development. “We now have close to 600 stores, through which we have been able to support Romanian producers. The vast majority of our fresh products come from Romania, as do our own-brand products.” He also stressed the extent to which the company’s local operations have developed beyond the initial investment model. “Auchan is a French group, but Auchan Romania has been built by Romanians, for Romanians.” For Danetiu, the impact of investment is also visible in the people trained by the company over the years, including employees who later took their experience into other sectors of the economy. Digital infrastructure becomes part of physical development Lucian Enaru focused on the increasingly technological nature of large commercial and industrial projects. Schneider Electric has been involved both in the original development of Sun Plaza and in its current modernisation. “Projects such as Sun Plaza are now designed and implemented digitally, using cloud infrastructure and digital twins that allow us to simulate costs, comfort, safety and different operating scenarios.” The change illustrates how physical infrastructure is becoming inseparable from digital systems, with design, energy management and operational decisions increasingly supported by connected equipment and real-time data. “Romania is at the forefront of innovation through projects like these.” Enaru also pointed to a second infrastructure challenge created by the rapid growth of AI and connected devices: data centres. With close to 20 billion devices connected globally, rising computing demand requires considerably more data-centre capacity. Romania currently has approximately 100 MW of such capacity, according to Enaru, with much of the existing market consisting of relatively small facilities. The main constraint for larger developments is increasingly the infrastructure surrounding computing rather than computing itself. “The biggest issue in a data centre today is cooling, rather than processing capacity or even energy. For a large data centre in Romania, finding the necessary power can also be difficult.” He argued that renewable generation can support further development, but data centres require continuous supply and therefore need a balanced energy mix. Bosch sees Romania as more than a low-cost manufacturing base İlker Kuşoğlu said Bosch employs around 6,000 people in its Romanian factories and will mark 30 years of local operations in 2027. For Kuşoğlu, Romania’s competitive case has to move beyond the traditional idea of a lower-cost production location. “Romania should not be seen simply as a low-cost location, but as one of the best locations for industry.” He identified talent as one of the country’s strongest assets, noting Bosch’s long-term partnerships with schools and universities and the evolution of its Romanian activities from conventional production technologies towards AI-enabled operations. “We are here to stay, we have long-term partnerships with schools and universities, and the quality of the workforce remains very high.” At the same time, he stressed the importance of long-term planning and predictability, particularly when Romania competes with markets such as China, where industrial strategies can operate over 10- or 20-year horizons. “If Romania cannot compete with China, then no country can.” CEE benefits as companies reconsider production footprints Gijs Klomp linked Romania’s opportunity to a wider shift in European manufacturing. WDP currently has roughly 2 million square metres of space in Romania, with automotive companies representing an important part of its tenant base. “Western companies operating globally need high-quality production space to remain competitive, and that is why we continue to see manufacturing moving towards Central and Eastern Europe.” For Romania, capturing a larger share of that investment will require maintaining the balance between cost, workforce quality, infrastructure and economic predictability. The panel suggested that Romania’s industrial proposition is becoming considerably more complex than labour-cost arbitrage. Retail assets need constant reinvention, factories require increasingly sophisticated technology and skills, logistics property follows changing production networks, while energy and digital infrastructure have become fundamental inputs into almost every investment decision.
